Circuit probing uncovers circuits responsible for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora in GPT2-Small and Medium.
Circuit probing is more faithful to the underlying model computation than linear probing, nonlinear probing, and amnesic probing.
papers.limitation: Neurons are typically polysemantic, so the assumption that a circuit is only causally implicated in computing a single intermediate variable may not hold completely.
papers.abstract: Neural network models have achieved high performance on a wide variety of complex tasks, but the algorithms that they implement are notoriously difficult to interpret. It is often necessary to hypothesize intermediate variables involved in a network's computation in order to understand these algorithms. For example, does a language model depend on particular syntactic properties when generating a sentence? Yet, existing analysis tools make it difficult to test hypotheses of this type. We propose a new analysis technique - circuit probing - that automatically uncovers low-level circuits that compute hypothesized intermediate variables. This enables causal analysis through targeted ablation at the level of model parameters. We apply this method to models trained on simple arithmetic tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness at (1) deciphering the algorithms that models have learned, (2) revealing modular structure within a model, and (3) tracking the development of circuits over training. Across these three experiments we demonstrate that circuit probing combines and extends the capabilities of existing methods, providing one unified approach for a variety of analyses. Finally, we demonstrate circuit probing on a real-world use case: uncovering circuits that are responsible for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora in GPT2-Small and Medium.

papers.title: InversionView: A General-Purpose Method for Reading Information from Neural Activations
papers.research_question: How can we decipher the information encoded in neural activations? The paper proposes InversionView, a method to sample from the preimage of an activation to uncover the information content.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces InversionView, a method that samples from the preimage of an activation via a conditional decoder to uncover the information encoded in neural activations and understand model algorithms.
papers.conclusion: InversionView is a general-purpose method that effectively deciphers information in neural activations, enabling better understanding of model algorithms and simplifying interpretability workflows.
papers.key_findings:
InversionView can reveal both basic and complex information in activations, such as token counts and relative positions.
InversionView simplifies interpretability workflows, agreeing with prior circuit findings in GPT-2 small.
InversionView enabled the first fully verified circuit for a 3-digit addition model.
InversionView scales to larger models like GPT-2 for factual recall.
papers.limitation:
Training a decoder requires a dataset of activations and can be computationally expensive.
The decoder may not perfectly capture the preimage, leading to potential biases in the generated samples.
The method is currently limited to discrete sequences (text).
future_direction: Extend InversionView to continuous domains.
Improve decoder efficiency.
Automate interpretation using LLMs.
papers.abstract: The inner workings of neural networks can be better understood if we can fully decipher the information encoded in neural activations. In this paper, we argue that this information is embodied by the subset of inputs that give rise to similar activations. We propose InversionView, which allows us to practically inspect this subset by sampling from a trained decoder model conditioned on activations. This helps uncover the information content of activation vectors, and facilitates understanding of the algorithms implemented by transformer models. We present four case studies where we investigate models ranging from small transformers to GPT-2. In these studies, we show that InversionView can reveal clear information contained in activations, including basic information about tokens appearing in the context, as well as more complex information, such as the count of certain tokens, their relative positions, and abstract knowledge about the subject. We also provide causally verified circuits to confirm the decoded information.

papers.title: Does injecting linguistic structure into language models lead to better alignment with brain recordings?
papers.research_question: Does injecting linguistic structure into language models lead to better alignment with brain recordings?
papers.core_contribution: Injecting linguistic structure bias into language models via guided attention during fine-tuning can improve alignment with brain recordings, particularly for word-level fMRI data.
papers.conclusion: Injecting linguistic structure bias through guided attention can improve brain decoding performance, with clearer benefits for finer-grained (word-level) analyses, and highlights the importance of controlling for domain effects.
papers.key_findings:
For the word-level Wehbe2014 fMRI dataset, guided attention models significantly outperform pretrained and domain-finetuned baselines in brain decoding.
For the sentence-level Pereira2018 dataset, improvements are more modest, with UD and DM guided attention models showing some improvement over the pretrained baseline.
Domain of the fine-tuning data is an important confound affecting brain alignment; simply fine-tuning on a different domain can reduce alignment.
Guided attention models perform better on subject-verb agreement syntactic probing tasks, with performance ranking corresponding to brain decoding scores.
Guided attention improves performance on a semantic tagging task for most semantic categories, especially discourse and temporal relations.
papers.limitation:
The fMRI data was recorded during passive reading without a specific task, which may limit the ability to uncover fine-grained patterns of linguistic structure.
Potential confounds such as domain, corpus size, and dependency length differences between the linguistic formalisms are not fully controlled for due to the lack of a common annotated corpus.
future_direction: Investigating brain alignment using continuous, naturalistic listening fMRI datasets.
Using a common annotated corpus for all formalisms to properly control for confounds like domain and corpus size.
papers.abstract: Neuroscientists evaluate deep neural networks for natural language processing as possible candidate models for how language is processed in the brain. These models are often trained without explicit linguistic supervision, but have been shown to learn some linguistic structure in the absence of such supervision (Manning et al., 2020), potentially questioning the relevance of symbolic linguistic theories in modeling such cognitive processes (Warstadt and Bowman, 2020). We evaluate across two fMRI datasets whether language models align better with brain recordings, if their attention is biased by annotations from syntactic or semantic formalisms. Using structure from dependency or minimal recursion semantic annotations, we find alignments improve significantly for one of the datasets. For another dataset, we see more mixed results. We present an extensive analysis of these results. Our proposed approach enables the evaluation of more targeted hypotheses about the composition of meaning in the brain, expanding the range of possible scientific inferences a neuroscientist could make, and opens up new opportunities for cross-pollination between computational neuroscience and linguistics.

papers.title: Who Reasons in the Large Language Models?
papers.research_question: A critical open question is whether reasoning abilities stem from the entire model, specific modules, or are merely artifacts of overfitting.
papers.core_contribution: The paper hypothesizes that the output projection (o_proj) in the Transformer's multi-head self-attention is primarily responsible for reasoning capabilities in LLMs, and introduces Stethoscope for Networks (SfN), a suite of diagnostic tools to probe and analyze internal behaviors, providing evidence for this hypothesis.
papers.conclusion: The work hypothesizes that the output projection (o_proj) module plays a central role in enabling reasoning capabilities in LLMs. The proposed Stethoscope for Networks (SfN) provides diagnostic tools that offer evidence for this hypothesis and open new directions for efficient and modular LLM training.
papers.key_findings:
The o_proj module exhibits the largest or second-largest weight changes during reasoning fine-tuning across model sizes (Delta Stethoscope).
Merging only the o_proj modules from a reasoning model into a base model can improve reasoning ability without further tuning (Merge Stethoscope).
Fine-tuning only o_proj (and layernorm, embed_tokens, lm_head) can achieve strong reasoning performance, with faster training and lower memory usage compared to full fine-tuning (Freeze Stethoscope).
Destroying o_proj does not harm conversational ability, while destroying MLP components or q/k_proj severely degrades it, suggesting a division of labor (Destruction Stethoscope).
The findings suggest o_proj is crucial for reasoning, while other modules primarily support conversational fluency.
papers.limitation:
Findings are primarily based on a limited set of model families and reasoning benchmarks, and may not generalize to all architectures or tasks.
Some diagnostic results rely on qualitative assessments rather than statistical validation.
A theoretical understanding of o_proj's function in reasoning remains to be established.
papers.abstract: Despite the impressive performance of large language models (LLMs), the process of endowing them with new capabilities--such as mathematical reasoning--remains largely empirical and opaque. A critical open question is whether reasoning abilities stem from the entire model, specific modules, or are merely artifacts of overfitting. In this work, we hypothesize that the reasoning capabilities in well-trained LLMs are primarily attributed to the output projection module (oproj) in the Transformer's multi-head self-attention (MHSA) mechanism. To support this hypothesis, we introduce Stethoscope for Networks (SfN), a suite of diagnostic tools designed to probe and analyze the internal behaviors of LLMs. Using SfN, we provide both circumstantial and empirical evidence suggesting that oproj plays a central role in enabling reasoning, whereas other modules contribute more to fluent dialogue. These findings offer a new perspective on LLM interpretability and open avenues for more targeted training strategies, potentially enabling more efficient and specialized LLMs.

papers.title: Correspondence between the layered structure of deep language models and temporal structure of natural language processing in the human brain
papers.research_question: Does the layered hierarchy of deep language models (DLMs) correspond to the temporal dynamics of language comprehension in the human brain? Specifically, is there a correlation between DLM layer depth and the time at which layers are most predictive of human brain activity?
papers.core_contribution: The layered hierarchy of deep language models (specifically GPT2-XL) corresponds to the temporal dynamics of language comprehension in the human brain, with early layers predicting early neural responses and later layers predicting later responses in high-order language areas.
papers.conclusion: The internal sequence of computations across layers in deep language models models the temporal hierarchy of language comprehension in the human brain, providing evidence for shared computational principles between DLMs and the brain.
papers.key_findings:
There is a strong positive correlation (Pearson r=0.85 in IFG) between DLM layer depth and the time of peak encoding performance in high-order language areas (IFG, TP, aSTG).
Intermediate layers of GPT2-XL (e.g., layer 22 in IFG) provide the best overall prediction of neural activity across language areas, forming an inverted U-shaped curve.
For predictable words, the temporal sequence is clear; for unpredictable words, the pattern is weaker and early layers shift to later lags (around 300ms) in IFG.
The temporal progression timescale increases along the ventral linguistic hierarchy, with the largest within-ROI temporal separation in the Temporal Pole (over 500 ms).
The observed lag-layer correlation is due to nonlinear transformations in the DLM, as linear interpolations between first and last layer embeddings yield significantly lower correlations.
papers.limitation:
The study uses a single DLM (GPT2-XL) and a single narrative stimulus, limiting generalizability.
The temporal resolution of the ECoG measurements, although high, was binned at 50 ms, which may not disambiguate layers that peak at similar times.
The hierarchical structure of DLMs is spatial, while that of the brain is spatiotemporal, representing a fundamental architectural difference.
future_direction: Explore other model architectures (e.g., recurrent, convolutional, or models with explicit temporal dynamics) to see if they better capture brain dynamics.
Use longer contexts and more diverse stimuli to test the robustness of the layer-time correspondence.
Investigate how DLMs might be augmented (e.g., with recurrence or explicit temporal hierarchies) to better model the brain's spatiotemporal language processing.
papers.abstract: Abstract Deep language models (DLMs) provide a novel computational paradigm for how the brain processes natural language. Unlike symbolic, rule-based models described in psycholinguistics, DLMs encode words and their context as continuous numerical vectors. These “embeddings” are constructed by a sequence of computations organized in “layers” to ultimately capture surprisingly sophisticated representations of linguistic structures. How does this layered hierarchy map onto the human brain during natural language comprehension? In this study, we used electrocorticography (ECoG) to record neural activity in language areas along the superior temporal gyrus and inferior frontal gyrus while human participants listened to a 30-minute spoken narrative. We supplied this same narrative to a high-performing DLM (GPT2-XL) and extracted the contextual embeddings for each word in the story across all 48 layers of the model. We next trained a set of linear encoding models to predict the temporally-evolving neural activity from the embeddings at each layer. We found a striking correspondence between the layer-by-layer sequence of embeddings from GPT2-XL and the temporal sequence of neural activity in language areas. In addition, we found evidence for the gradual accumulation of recurrent information along the linguistic processing hierarchy. However, we also noticed additional neural processes in the brain, but not in DLMs, during the processing of surprising (unpredictable) words. These findings point to a connection between human language processing and DLMs where the layer-by-layer accumulation of contextual information in DLM embeddings matches the temporal dynamics of neural activity in high-order language areas.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: Diverging views on the role of structured representations in linguistics and language modeling
papers.research_question: How do language models compare to human language processing in terms of structured representations, and what is their role in the science of language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that language models struggle with structured representations central to human language, and suggests that for language models to be effective models of language, structured representations must be incorporated as computational objects.
papers.conclusion: Language models need to conceptualize structured representations as computational objects to better align with human language and contribute to the science of language.
papers.key_findings:
Language models trained on next-word prediction may not learn structure-dependent representations necessary for human language.
Models like ChatGPT show insensitivity to Binding Principle C, incorrectly allowing co-reference in prohibited contexts.
Language models do not make a qualitative distinction between possible and impossible languages, treating them similarly unlike humans.
The internal representational infrastructure for possible and impossible languages overlaps in models, indicating no fundamental difference.
Incorporating structured representations as primary computational targets could enhance language models' utility as models of language.
future_direction: Incorporate structured representations as computational objects in language modeling.
papers.abstract: Recent years have seen dramatic advances in the linguistic abilities of language models, leading some authors to argue that they can be treated as models of language. Against this background, we provide a cognitive perspective on the place of language models in the science of language, with a particular focus on the role of structured representations. Evidence from linguistics, psychology and cognitive neuroscience shows that structured representations occupy a central place in the human mind. Structured representations constrain how linguistic forms map onto meanings, thereby determining the boundaries of possible human languages. In language modeling, instead, the place of structured representations is often peripheral. They are seen as optional end point of modeling, to be induced as a consequence of the objective the model tries to optimize – that is, next-word prediction. Because structured relations and representations are not necessarily useful for predicting the next word in a sequence, it is not guaranteed that the model’s internal organization will come to encode those representations. Indeed, contemporary language models struggle to use structured representations functionally to map form onto meaning, and to determine whether they should consider their input as a possible human language or not. Building on classic insights in linguistics and (computational) cognitive science, we suggest that any use of language models as models of language requires conceptualizing the role of structured representations as computational objects.

papers.title: When Less Language is More: Language-Reasoning Disentanglement Makes LLMs Better Multilingual Reasoners
papers.research_question: Can reasoning and language processing in LLMs be disentangled to improve multilingual reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that reasoning and language can be disentangled in LLMs by ablating language-specific components in hidden states, leading to improved multilingual reasoning performance across diverse models and languages.
papers.conclusion: The findings demonstrate that language and reasoning are separable in LLMs, and the proposed training-free intervention provides a lightweight and interpretable strategy for improving cross-lingual generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Language-reasoning disentanglement via activation ablation consistently improves multilingual reasoning performance across 10 open-weight LLMs and 11 typologically diverse languages.
There is a negative correlation between language-specific activation and reasoning accuracy; removing language-specific signals improves reasoning.
Middle layers are most effective for disentanglement, improving reasoning while preserving language fidelity, whereas upper-layer ablation degrades output fluency.
The training-free intervention achieves comparable or superior results to post-training methods like supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.
Low-resource languages show a trade-off: reasoning improves with ablation, but language fidelity drops more sharply than in high-resource languages.
papers.limitation:
After ablation, models tend to default to English, which may reduce language fidelity, especially for low-resource languages.
The exact ratios of pretraining data for different languages are unknown, which limits a definitive explanation of the convergence phenomenon.
future_direction: Further investigation into the convergence of non-English representations to English after ablation.
Exploring adaptive ablation strategies to balance reasoning improvement and language fluency for low-resource languages.
Combining the training-free intervention with post-training methods for enhanced multilingual reasoning.
papers.abstract: Multilingual reasoning remains a significant challenge for large language models (LLMs), with performance disproportionately favoring high-resource languages. Drawing inspiration from cognitive neuroscience, which suggests that human reasoning functions largely independently of language processing, we hypothesize that LLMs similarly encode reasoning and language as separable components that can be disentangled to enhance multilingual reasoning. To evaluate this, we perform a causal intervention by ablating language-specific representations at inference time. Experiments on 10 open-weight LLMs spanning 11 typologically diverse languages show that this language-specific ablation consistently boosts multilingual reasoning performance. Layer-wise analyses further confirm that language and reasoning representations can be effectively disentangled throughout the model, yielding improved multilingual reasoning capabilities, while preserving top-layer language features remains essential for maintaining linguistic fidelity. Compared to post-training methods such as supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning, our training-free language-reasoning disentanglement achieves comparable or superior results with minimal computational overhead. These findings shed light on the internal mechanisms underlying multilingual reasoning in LLMs and suggest a lightweight and interpretable strategy for improving cross-lingual generalization.

papers.title: LLM world models are mental: Output layer evidence of brittle world model use in LLM mechanical reasoning
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) construct and manipulate internal 'world models,' or do they rely solely on statistical associations represented as output layer token probabilities learned from data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs show some ability to reason about mechanical systems (pulley systems) using heuristics like pulley counting and can differentiate functional from jumbled systems, but their internal representations are brittle and fail when the task requires understanding of nuanced structural connectivity, indicating limited world model use.
papers.conclusion: The findings offer mixed support for the view that LLMs reason over world models independently from output token probabilities. The brittleness of these representations, especially in Study 3, aligns with critiques emphasizing the lack of robustness and generality in current systems.
papers.key_findings:
In Study 1, LLMs performed above chance in estimating mechanical advantage (MA) and their estimates correlated with ground truth MA, but they relied on a pulley-counting heuristic and selectively attended to relevant features.
LLMs could distinguish functional from non-functional (jumbled) pulley systems with high accuracy (F1=0.8) in Study 2.
In Study 3, LLMs failed to differentiate functional from non-functional (but connected) pulley systems, performing at chance level (F1=0.46).
The results suggest LLMs have some latent knowledge of pulley systems but lack robust internal models for nuanced structural reasoning.
The brittleness of these representations aligns with critiques emphasizing the lack of robustness and generality in current systems.
papers.limitation:
Uncertainty regarding whether tested pulley stimuli are truly out-of-distribution; exposure during training cannot be ruled out.
Difficulty deconfounding output layer token representations from potential latent world models represented in network weights without combining with interpretability research.
future_direction: Future work should further deconfound pulley count from MA and employ novel or synthetic diagramming languages to limit reliance on familiar formats like TikZ.
Extending the paradigm to other physical systems (e.g., levers, gear trains) may help assess the breadth of these internal representations.
Integrating the present approach with interpretability research may help elucidate the network circuits underlying reasoning over world models.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) construct and manipulate internal world models, or do they rely solely on statistical associations represented as output layer token probabilities? We adapt cognitive science methodologies from human mental models research to test LLMs on pulley system problems using TikZ-rendered stimuli. Study 1 examines whether LLMs can estimate mechanical advantage (MA). State-of-the-art models performed marginally but significantly above chance, and their estimates correlated significantly with ground-truth MA. Significant correlations between number of pulleys and model estimates suggest that models employed a pulley counting heuristic, without necessarily simulating pulley systems to derive precise values. Study 2 tested this by probing whether LLMs represent global features crucial to MA estimation. Models evaluated a functionally connected pulley system against a fake system with randomly placed components. Without explicit cues, models identified the functional system as having greater MA with F1=0.8, suggesting LLMs could represent systems well enough to differentiate jumbled from functional systems. Study 3 built on this by asking LLMs to compare functional systems with matched systems which were connected up but which transferred no force to the weight; LLMs identified the functional system with F1=0.46, suggesting random guessing. Insofar as they may generalize, these findings are compatible with the notion that LLMs manipulate internal world models, sufficient to exploit statistical associations between pulley count and MA (Study 1), and to approximately represent system components' spatial relations (Study 2). However, they may lack the facility to reason over nuanced structural connectivity (Study 3). We conclude by advocating the utility of cognitive scientific methods to evaluate the world-modeling capacities of artificial intelligence systems.

papers.title: Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations: Understanding Belief Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal belief representations emerge in language models? Are they structured or spurious? How robust are they to prompt variations? Can they be strengthened?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that belief representations in language models improve with model size and fine-tuning, are structured yet brittle to prompt variations, and can be strengthened using contrastive activation addition to correct wrong Theory of Mind inferences.
papers.conclusion: Belief representations in language models are structured but brittle, and they can be strengthened via activation editing, offering a path toward more reliable Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Belief representations emerge in consistent patterns across models, improve with model size, and benefit significantly from fine-tuning, especially in smaller models.
Control tasks and PCA show that belief representations are structured and not spurious.
Representations of others' beliefs are brittle to semantically neutral prompt variations.
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) can strengthen belief representations and improve ToM performance across different tasks.
CAA steering vectors are general and transferable to other ToM tasks, yielding substantial performance gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focused on one dataset (BigToM) and a limited set of model families due to computational constraints.
The approach could be extended to other mental states beyond beliefs.
future_direction: Exploring how different types of fine-tuning influence the emergence of internal belief representations.
Developing robustness benchmarks and new approaches to improve generalization of belief representations.
Directly embedding perspective-taking circuits into model architectures.
papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in Theory of Mind (ToM) tasks for evaluating language models (LMs), little is known about how LMs internally represent mental states of self and others. Understanding these internal mechanisms is critical - not only to move beyond surface-level performance, but also for model alignment and safety, where subtle misattributions of mental states may go undetected in generated outputs. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of belief representations in LMs by probing models across different scales, training regimens, and prompts - using control tasks to rule out confounds. Our experiments provide evidence that both model size and fine-tuning substantially improve LMs' internal representations of others' beliefs, which are structured - not mere by-products of spurious correlations - yet brittle to prompt variations. Crucially, we show that these representations can be strengthened: targeted edits to model activations can correct wrong ToM inferences.

papers.title: Do LLMs Know about Hallucination? An Empirical Investigation of LLM's Hidden States
papers.research_question: Do LLMs possess awareness of hallucination, and if so, to what extent and through what mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Provides empirical evidence that LLMs exhibit awareness of hallucination through differences in hidden states when processing correct vs hallucinated answers, and shows potential for using hidden state guidance to mitigate hallucination.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess awareness of hallucination as evidenced by differences in hidden states, and leveraging hidden state guidance can help mitigate hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
LLM’s final hidden state is more susceptible to be influenced by a correct answer compared to a hallucinated one.
Strategically inducing an LLM to produce hallucinated responses can raise its awareness consequently.
The level of awareness corresponds to the uncertainty of the LLM in the responses.
Providing relevant knowledge can assist LLMs in identifying hallucinated responses.
The transition between hidden states encodes truthfulness information.
papers.limitation:
Do not differentiate between fine-grained categories of hallucination.
Do not examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers, only the final layer.
Experiments are performed on conventional QA tasks, not more complicated or domain-specific tasks.
Future research is needed to develop more effective strategies for mitigating LLM hallucination.
future_direction: Explore different types of hallucination (factual fabrication, instruction inconsistency, etc.).
Examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers and investigate layer-by-layer formation of hallucination.
Adapt the experimental framework to more complicated or domain-specific tasks and potentially extend to multimodal features.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can make up answers that are not real, and this is known as hallucination. This research aims to see if, how, and to what extent LLMs are aware of hallucination. More specifically, we check whether and how an LLM reacts differently in its hidden states when it answers a question right versus when it hallucinates. To do this, we introduce an experimental framework which allows examining LLM's hidden states in different hallucination situations. Building upon this framework, we conduct a series of experiments with language models in the LLaMA family (Touvron et al., 2023). Our empirical findings suggest that LLMs react differently when processing a genuine response versus a fabricated one. We then apply various model interpretation techniques to help understand and explain the findings better. Moreover, informed by the empirical observations, we show great potential of using the guidance derived from LLM's hidden representation space to mitigate hallucination. We believe this work provides insights into how LLMs produce hallucinated answers and how to make them occur less often.

papers.title: How Syntax Specialization Emerges in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does syntactic specialization emerge and evolve over training, and how do model initialization, scale, and training data shape this development?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Syntactic Sensitivity Index (SSI) to measure syntactic specialization in language models, revealing that syntactic sensitivity emerges gradually, concentrates in specific layers, exhibits a critical period, and is consistent across architectures but implemented by different neurons.
papers.conclusion: Provides the first systematic, mechanistic account of how syntactic specialization emerges in transformer language models by introducing SSI and applying it across training trajectories, seeds, and model scales, offering an integrated picture of when, where, and how syntax is represented.
papers.key_findings:
SSI correlates with grammaticality judgment accuracy and outperforms supervised probing methods like SVM and regression.
Syntactic specialization emerges gradually during training, with different syntactic phenomena showing distinct acquisition timelines and layer profiles.
There is a critical period (around 16 million tokens) during which syntactic specialization rapidly emerges and then stabilizes.
While layer-level syntactic representations converge across different random seeds, the specific neurons responsible for syntax sensitivity differ (convergent layers, divergent neurons).
Larger models and more training data enhance syntactic abstraction and specialization, but the effect varies across syntactic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Relies on sentence embeddings (mean pooling) which may miss token-level nuance or positional dynamics.
BLiMP focuses on binary acceptability, leaving gradient judgments, semantic-pragmatic interactions, and multi-sentence structures underexplored.
Open theoretical questions about minimal inductive bias, architectural interventions, and relation to semantic grounding.
future_direction: Extend SSI to token-level activations or attention maps.
Explore gradient judgments, semantic-pragmatic interactions, and multi-sentence structures beyond binary acceptability.
Investigate the minimal inductive bias or data regime required for syntactic specialization, architectural interventions, and how syntactic development relates to semantic grounding.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been found to develop surprising internal specializations: Individual neurons, attention heads, and circuits become selectively sensitive to syntactic structure, reflecting patterns observed in the human brain. While this specialization is well-documented, how it emerges during training and what influences its development remains largely unknown. In this work, we tap into the black box of specialization by tracking its formation over time. By quantifying internal syntactic consistency across minimal pairs from various syntactic phenomena, we identify a clear developmental trajectory: Syntactic sensitivity emerges gradually, concentrates in specific layers, and exhibits a 'critical period' of rapid internal specialization. This process is consistent across architectures and initialization parameters (e.g., random seeds), and is influenced by model scale and training data. We therefore reveal not only where syntax arises in LLMs but also how some models internalize it during training. To support future research, we will release the code, models, and training checkpoints upon acceptance.

papers.title: Exploring the LLM Journey from Cognition to Expression with Linear Representations
papers.research_question: How do cognitive and expressive capabilities develop and interact in large language models across pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback stages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cognitive capabilities in LLMs are established during pretraining, while expressive capabilities develop during SFT and RLHF, with cognitive capability setting an upper bound for expressive capability.
papers.conclusion: This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of LLM training processes.
papers.key_findings:
Cognitive capability is primarily established during the pretraining stage, whereas expressive capability develops during SFT and RLHF.
There is a strong statistical correlation between cognitive and expressive capabilities, with cognitive capability acting as an upper bound.
The gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities can be bridged by optimization-free methods such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling.
The vocabulary linear layer plays a crucial role in expressive capability, and its training during SFT/RLHF helps reduce the gap.
Layer-wise analysis reveals a plateau in cognitive capability in deeper layers, indicating redundancy in the model architecture.
future_direction: Exploring additional linear analysis techniques for model analysis and control.
papers.abstract: This paper presents an in-depth examination of the evolution and interplay of cognitive and expressive capabilities in large language models (LLMs), with a specific focus on Baichuan-7B and Baichuan-33B, an advanced bilingual (Chinese and English) LLM series. We define and explore the model's cognitive and expressive capabilities through linear representations across three critical phases: Pretraining, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Cognitive capability is defined as the quantity and quality of information conveyed by the neuron output vectors within the network, similar to the neural signal processing in human cognition. Expressive capability is defined as the model's capability to produce word-level output. Our findings unveil a sequential development pattern, where cognitive abilities are largely established during Pretraining, whereas expressive abilities predominantly advance during SFT and RLHF. Statistical analyses confirm a significant correlation between the two capabilities, suggesting that cognitive capacity may limit expressive potential. The paper also explores the theoretical underpinnings of these divergent developmental trajectories and their connection to the LLMs' architectural design. Moreover, we evaluate various optimization-independent strategies, such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling, which bridge the gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities. This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of their training processes.

papers.title: Grokked Transformers are Implicit Reasoners: A Mechanistic Journey to the Edge of Generalization
papers.research_question: Can transformers learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge, and how does grokking enable this? What are the differences in systematic generalization between composition and comparison tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge through grokking, but systematic generalization varies: composition fails out-of-distribution while comparison succeeds. Mechanistic analysis reveals the formation of generalizing circuits and explains the differences, guiding data and training setups and suggesting architectural improvements.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are capable of learning implicit reasoning through grokking, but the level of systematic generalization depends on the task and the circuit configuration. The findings guide data and training setups and suggest improvements to the transformer architecture for better cross-layer memory sharing.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can learn implicit reasoning only through grokking (extended training far beyond overfitting).
The speed of grokking correlates with the ratio of inferred to atomic facts (data distribution), not the absolute training data size.
For composition, transformers fail to generalize systematically to out-of-distribution examples, while for comparison, they succeed.
Mechanistic analysis reveals distinct generalizing circuits: for composition, a sequential circuit that stores atomic facts in separate layers; for comparison, a parallel circuit that stores atomic facts in the same layer.
In a complex reasoning task with a large search space, a fully grokked transformer achieves near-perfect accuracy, while state-of-the-art LLMs with non-parametric memory (GPT-4-Turbo, Gemini-1.5-Pro) fail regardless of prompting or retrieval augmentation.
papers.limitation:
The task formulation (induction and application of inference rules from atomic and inferred facts) may not apply to the full spectrum of reasoning types.
The study is limited to synthetic tasks and may not fully capture real-world reasoning complexities.
future_direction: Developing cross-layer memory-sharing mechanisms for transformers (e.g., memory-augmentation, explicit recurrence) to improve systematic generalization.
Investigating the tradeoff between parametric and non-parametric memory in language models.
Understanding the role of verbalizations (e.g., chain-of-thought) in teaching models to reason implicitly.
papers.abstract: We study whether transformers can learn to implicitly reason over parametric knowledge, a skill that even the most capable language models struggle with. Focusing on two representative reasoning types, composition and comparison, we consistently find that transformers can learn implicit reasoning, but only through grokking, i.e., extended training far beyond overfitting. The levels of generalization also vary across reasoning types: when faced with out-of-distribution examples, transformers fail to systematically generalize for composition but succeed for comparison. We delve into the model's internals throughout training, conducting analytical experiments that reveal: 1) the mechanism behind grokking, such as the formation of the generalizing circuit and its relation to the relative efficiency of generalizing and memorizing circuits, and 2) the connection between systematicity and the configuration of the generalizing circuit. Our findings guide data and training setup to better induce implicit reasoning and suggest potential improvements to the transformer architecture, such as encouraging cross-layer knowledge sharing. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for a challenging reasoning task with a large search space, GPT-4-Turbo and Gemini-1.5-Pro based on non-parametric memory fail badly regardless of prompting styles or retrieval augmentation, while a fully grokked transformer can achieve near-perfect accuracy, showcasing the power of parametric memory for complex reasoning.

papers.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The model performs genuine two-hop reasoning with intermediate steps, such as representing 'Texas' when answering about the capital of the state containing Dallas.
In poetry generation, the model plans ahead by pre-selecting rhyming words before writing each line.
Multilingual circuits use a mix of language-specific and abstract, language-independent components, with more abstraction in larger models.
Entity recognition circuits distinguish known and unknown entities, influencing when the model answers or refuses, with circuit misfires causing hallucinations.
Refusal mechanisms involve harmful request features aggregated from pretraining and trigger refusal during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
tools provide satisfying insight for about a quarter of prompts
replacement model incompletely and imperfectly captures the original model
future_direction: Developing more effective unsupervised exploration tools for increasingly capable models
papers.abstract: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs? This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability. Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.

papers.title: Ungrammatical Influences: Evidence for Dynamical Language Processing
papers.research_question: Do ungrammatical influences exist in human sentence processing? Specifically, are readers temporarily distracted by coherent but grammatically incompatible local structures during parsing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence from a connectionist model and human reading experiments that ungrammatical local structures can influence parsing, supporting a dynamical, self-organizing approach to language processing.
papers.conclusion: Ungrammatical influences exist in human sentence processing, and dynamical, self-organizing models like connectionist networks can account for these effects, pointing towards parallel processing solutions to parsing tractability.
papers.key_findings:
A Simple Recurrent Network model shows higher error (Kullback-Leibler Divergence) on sentences containing irrelevant local coherences (e.g., noun-noun compounds) that are grammatically incompatible with the global structure.
Human reading times are slower for sentences containing such ungrammatical local coherences (Experiment 1), indicating distraction by grammatically ruled-out interpretations.
A stronger slowing effect is found for reduced relative clauses with homophonous verbs compared to non-homophonous verbs (Experiment 2), showing the effect extends beyond lexical compounds.
The results suggest that parsing involves competition among local coherences via dynamical feedback, rather than deductive elimination of parses based on top-down constraints.
The connectionist model's behavior aligns with human data, indicating that dynamical, self-organizing mechanisms may address tractability problems in parsing.
papers.limitation:
The effect in the network simulation was somewhat unstable with longer training on the same materials and sometimes reversed itself.
Experiment 1 results could be explained by lexical automaticity (activation of compound senses in the lexicon) rather than syntactic parsing interference, though Experiment 2 addresses this.
future_direction: Further exploration of dynamical parsing models that use feedback and self-organization to handle incoherent structure representation.
Incorporating the problem of incoherent structure representation into the theory of grammar.
papers.abstract: Ungrammatical Inuences: Evidence for Dynamical Language Processing Whitney Tabor tabor@uconnvm.uconn.edu Bruno Galantucci Bruno.Galantucci@uconn.edu Department of Psychology University of Connecticut Storrs, CT 06269 USA Abstract A distinguishing feature of self-organizing models of cog- nitive structure is that they permit incompatible struc- tures to coexist at least temporarily. Here we report on a connectionist model of natural language process- ing which appears to temporarily construct incoherent structures. We then describe two reading-time studies which reveal people exhibiting the same tendency. In particular, both networks and people show sensitivity to the irrelevant structural interpretations of the under- lined phrases in (1) and (2). (1) We did not think the company would re truck drivers without consulting the union rst. (2) The manager watched the waiter served pea soup by the trainee. This kind of sensitivity is absent in parsing models which treat grammatical constraints as absolute because such models lack a principled method of generating incoher- ent parses. Connectionist networks make the right pre- dictions by using feedback and self-organization. Our results push in the direction of seeking a solution to the tractability problems of parsing by using dynamical mechanisms in a parallel architecture. Introduction Current sentence-processing research tends to focus on ambiguity-related processing in sentences like (1) { (3): (1) The mechanic maintained the truck was working beautifully. (2) The cop arrested by the detective was chagrined. (3) The cook stirred the soup with the tomatoes. Each of these sentences has a structural ambiguity which is resolved on the basis of structural or pragmatic infor- mation when the underlined words arrive. Reading time and eye tracking studies show that when biases favor the wrong interpretation initially, readers tend to slow down and/or make regressions in the disambiguating re- gion, which suggests that they either choose the wrong parse initially or are biased toward it (see Frazier, 1988; Tanenhaus & Trueswell, 1995). Such phenomena accord well with a model of sen- tence processing which assumes people construct phrase- structure parses incrementally based on the input up to the current point in time. On this view, the slow-down in the disambiguating region is due either to extra time Figure 1: The Zollner illusion. spent on revising an incorrect parse, or to extra time spent on revising the weighting assigned to dierent pos- sible parses maintained in parallel. Focusing for a moment on cognitive processes outside of sentence processing, there is a good deal of evidence that people are reliably vulnerable to certain adverse inuences when interpreting complex stimuli. In the Zollner illusion (Held, 1971|Figure 1), lines on a page appear to be nonparallel even though retinal and depth of eld information indicate parallelism. Similarly, in the Stroop eect (Stroop, 1966), a decision is supposed to have been made ahead of time to interpret the stimulus along one particular dimension of contrast (e.g. color), and yet when the stimulus is presented, people are often led astray by irrelevant verbal information. These cases are dierent from the classic sentence pro- cessing examples listed in (1) through (3) in that they show people temporarily failing to rule out an interpre- tation that could be ruled out absolutely, given the in- formation at hand. What would be the analogous cases in sentence processing? Denition of Ungrammatical Inuences There is a class of sentences in which one parse of a word sequence can be completely ruled out on grammatical grounds and yet (we hypothesize) people are inuenced by it anyway. The following are examples of such hy- pothesized \Ungrammatical Inuences : (4) a. They won't re truck drivers on Sunday. b. They won't hire truck drivers on Sunday.

papers.title: The Grammar-Learning Trajectories of Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: Do neural language models learn grammatical phenomena in a consistent order across different initializations, architectures, and training data? What does this consistency reveal about their inductive biases and linguistic representations?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models acquire grammatical phenomena in a consistent order across different initializations, architectures, and training data, indicating a shared inductive bias. The learning trajectory is approximately one-dimensional, meaning that overall performance predicts which linguistic generalizations have been acquired.
papers.conclusion: Studying learning trajectories is a promising approach to understand linguistic representations in NLMs, and the consistency suggests a mutual inductive bias that underlies these models' learning of linguistic phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
NLMs with different random initializations learn grammatical phenomena in a highly correlated order.
Different architectures (GPT2 and TransformerXL) also show similar learning trajectories when aligned by performance level.
The choice of training data has some effect but does not override the consistent ordering.
The learning trajectory is approximately one-dimensional: models with similar overall performance have similar performance on individual phenomena.
Early in training, NLMs rely on local cues and resemble bag-of-words models; later they become more sensitive to structural cues.
future_direction: Consider the impact of additional factors, architectures and learning phases that appear only later in training.
Develop a theory that can account for the patterns presented by NLMs’ learning trajectories.
papers.abstract: The learning trajectories of linguistic phenomena in humans provide insight into linguistic representation, beyond what can be gleaned from inspecting the behavior of an adult speaker. To apply a similar approach to analyze neural language models (NLM), it is first necessary to establish that different models are similar enough in the generalizations they make. In this paper, we show that NLMs with different initialization, architecture, and training data acquire linguistic phenomena in a similar order, despite their different end performance. These findings suggest that there is some mutual inductive bias that underlies these models' learning of linguistic phenomena. Taking inspiration from psycholinguistics, we argue that studying this inductive bias is an opportunity to study the linguistic representation implicit in NLMs.

papers.title: A Implies B: Circuit Analysis in LLMs for Propositional Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do large language models solve propositional logic problems? Are their reasoning mechanisms localized and modular, and what are the core components involved?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that LLMs use sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, consisting of four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating, queried-rule moving, fact processing, and decision making. These circuits are similar across different models but show scale-dependent variations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, with specialized attention head families. These circuits are similar across models but exhibit scale-dependent differences, suggesting that mechanistic insights do not fully generalize across model sizes.
papers.key_findings:
All three models contain four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating heads, queried-rule mover heads, fact-processing heads, and decision heads.
The models perform lazy reasoning: the core circuit activates primarily after seeing the Question and the query variable.
The models reuse sub-circuits for different parts of the argument when possible.
Gemma-2-27B has additional logical-operator heads and a more parallel circuit compared to the more sequential Gemma-2-9B.
Small trained models (3-layer) perform intermingled reasoning, less modular than larger pre-trained models.
papers.limitation: Partial analysis of Gemma-2-27B due to computational constraints
future_direction: Fully validating the algorithm for LogOp chain reasoning in small transformers
papers.abstract: Due to the size and complexity of modern large language models (LLMs), it has proven challenging to uncover the underlying mechanisms that models use to solve reasoning problems. For instance, is their reasoning for a specific problem localized to certain parts of the network? Do they break down the reasoning problem into modular components that are then executed as sequential steps as we go deeper in the model? To better understand the reasoning capability of LLMs, we study a minimal propositional logic problem that requires combining multiple facts to arrive at a solution. By studying this problem on Mistral and Gemma models, up to 27B parameters, we illuminate the core components the models use to solve such logic problems. From a mechanistic interpretability point of view, we use causal mediation analysis to uncover the pathways and components of the LLMs' reasoning processes. Then, we offer fine-grained insights into the functions of attention heads in different layers. We not only find a sparse circuit that computes the answer, but we decompose it into sub-circuits that have four distinct and modular uses. Finally, we reveal that three distinct models -- Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Gemma-2-27B -- contain analogous but not identical mechanisms.

papers.title: Scaling sparse feature circuit finding for in-context learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to understand the mechanism of in-context learning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify task-detection and task-execution features in the in-context learning circuit of large language models, and introduces the Task Vector Cleaning algorithm to decompose task vectors into interpretable features.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance understanding of in-context learning mechanisms and demonstrate the potential of sparse autoencoders as a powerful tool for interpretability research on larger language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can be used to analyze in-context learning in larger models like Gemma-1 2B, scaling up circuit analysis.
Task-execution features encode task knowledge and can causally induce task zero-shot performance.
Task-detection features identify tasks from the prompt and are causally linked to execution features via attention and MLP sublayers.
The Task Vector Cleaning algorithm effectively decomposes task vectors into sparse, interpretable features while preserving their effect on loss.
The in-context learning circuit involves interaction between detection and execution features through attention and MLP layers.
papers.limitation:
Circuit search was constrained to intermediate layers due to early layers processing token-level information and having lower quality Indirect Effect approximations.
Hundreds of features needed to be ablated to achieve significant faithfulness degradation, unlike prior work which required fewer.
Negative steering experiments showed lower task specificity, indicating steering experiments alone may not suffice for comprehensive analysis.
future_direction: Improving SAE training to yield more monosemantic features.
Scaling circuit analysis to even larger models.
Applying these techniques to more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular tool for interpreting large language model activations, but their utility in addressing open questions in interpretability remains unclear. In this work, we demonstrate their effectiveness by using SAEs to deepen our understanding of the mechanism behind in-context learning (ICL). We identify abstract SAE features that (i) encode the model's knowledge of which task to execute and (ii) whose latent vectors causally induce the task zero-shot. This aligns with prior work showing that ICL is mediated by task vectors. We further demonstrate that these task vectors are well approximated by a sparse sum of SAE latents, including these task-execution features. To explore the ICL mechanism, we adapt the sparse feature circuits methodology of Marks et al. (2024) to work for the much larger Gemma-1 2B model, with 30 times as many parameters, and to the more complex task of ICL. Through circuit finding, we discover task-detecting features with corresponding SAE latents that activate earlier in the prompt, that detect when tasks have been performed. They are causally linked with task-execution features through the attention and MLP sublayers.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: How transfer learning impacts linguistic knowledge in deep NLP models?
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning towards downstream NLP tasks impact the learned linguistic knowledge in pre-trained language models?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning redistributes linguistic knowledge in pre-trained language models, with BERT retaining it deeper in the network while RoBERTa and XLNet localize it to lower layers, and the effect varies across downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning causes linguistic knowledge to be preserved in higher layers for some tasks and forgotten in others, with architectural differences: BERT retains knowledge deeper, while RoBERTa and XLNet localize it to lower layers.
papers.key_findings:
For some GLUE tasks (e.g., STS, RTE, MRPC), linguistic knowledge is preserved in higher layers after fine-tuning, while for others (e.g., SST, QNLI, MNLI) it is forgotten in higher layers.
BERT retains linguistic knowledge deeper in the network after fine-tuning, while RoBERTa and XLNet delegate it predominantly to lower layers.
Linguistic information becomes less distributed and less redundant in the network after fine-tuning, especially in RoBERTa and XLNet.
Salient linguistic neurons shift from higher to lower layers after fine-tuning in RoBERTa and XLNet.
Pruning bottom layers in RoBERTa and XLNet leads to more performance degradation than in BERT, consistent with the localization of linguistic knowledge to lower layers.
future_direction: Connecting linguistic probes with causation analysis on these tasks.
Detailed exploration of layer pruning patterns.
papers.abstract: Transfer learning from pre-trained neural language models towards downstream tasks has been a predominant theme in NLP recently. Several researchers have shown that deep NLP models learn non-trivial amount of linguistic knowledge, captured at different layers of the model. We investigate how fine-tuning towards downstream NLP tasks impacts the learned linguistic knowledge. We carry out a study across popular pre-trained models BERT, RoBERTa and XLNet using layer and neuronlevel diagnostic classifiers. We found that for some GLUE tasks, the network relies on the core linguistic information and preserve it deeper in the network, while for others it forgets. Linguistic information is distributed in the pre-trained language models but becomes localized to the lower layers post-fine-tuning, reserving higher layers for the task specific knowledge. The pattern varies across architectures, with BERT retaining linguistic information relatively deeper in the network compared to RoBERTa and XLNet, where it is predominantly delegated to the lower layers.

papers.title: A Neurocomputational Model of Grounded Language Comprehension and Production at the Sentence Level
papers.research_question: How can a neural network learn to comprehend and produce sentence-level language grounded in a virtual environment, and what internal representations does it learn?
papers.core_contribution: The dissertation presents a neural network model that learns to map natural language questions to full-sentence answers using sublexical phoneme sequences, and introduces a novel training algorithm (LSTM-g) for second-order recurrent neural networks that uses only local computations.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation demonstrates that starting from a neural level can yield insights into cognitive representations and behaviors, and that the model provides a step towards more relatable and human-like language processing systems.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns combinatorial internal representations, enabling systematic generalization to novel sentences.
The model exhibits human-like critical period effects in second language acquisition when simulating memory development.
The LSTM-g training algorithm is effective and biologically plausible, requiring only local computations.
The model successfully grounds language in vision, learning to answer questions about a virtual environment.
The model learns via direct imitation of another speaker, emulating human language acquisition.
papers.limitation: The model uses a simplified virtual environment and a limited grammar, and does not handle complex sentences.
future_direction: Extend the model to more complex language and real-world perception.
Test the model on more psycholinguistic tasks to explore listener interpretations.
Investigate the emergence of syntax and other linguistic phenomena.
papers.abstract: While symbolic and statistical approaches to natural language processing have become undeniably impressive in recent years, such systems still display a tendency to make errors that are inscrutable to human onlookers. This disconnect with human processing may stem from the vast differences in the substrates that underly natural language processing in artificial systems versus biological systems. To create a more relatable system, this dissertation turns to the more biologically inspired substrate of neural networks, describing the design and implementation of a model that learns to comprehend and produce language at the sentence level. The model's task is to ground simulated speech streams, representing a simple subset of English, in terms of a virtual environment. The model learns to understand and answer full-sentence questions about the environment by mimicking the speech stream of another speaker, much as a human language learner would. It is the only known neural model to date that can learn to map natural language questions to full-sentence natural language answers, where both question and answer are represented sublexically as phoneme sequences. The model addresses important points for which most other models, neural and otherwise, fail to account. First, the model learns to ground its linguistic knowledge using human-like sensory representations, gaining language understanding at a deeper level than that of syntactic structure. Second, analysis provides evidence that the model learns combinatorial internal representations, thus gaining the compositionality of symbolic approaches to cognition, which is vital for computationally efficient encoding and decoding of meaning. The model does this while retaining the fully distributed representations characteristic of neural networks, providing the resistance to damage and graceful degradation that are generally lacking in symbolic and statistical approaches. Finally, the model learns via direct imitation of another speaker, allowing it to emulate human processing with greater fidelity, thus increasing the relatability of its behavior. Along the way, this dissertation develops a novel training algorithm that, for the first time, requires only local computations to train arbitrary second-order recurrent neural networks. This algorithm is evaluated on its overall efficacy, biological feasibility, and ability to reproduce peculiarities of human learning such as age-correlated effects in second language acquisition.

papers.title: Large Language Models are In-Context Semantic Reasoners rather than Symbolic Reasoners
papers.research_question: Are LLMs good in-context reasoners without semantics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that semantics are vital for LLMs' in-context reasoning; they perform well when semantics align with commonsense but struggle with symbolic or counter-commonsense reasoning, relying on superficial semantic connections rather than formal symbolic reasoning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs rely heavily on learned semantics for in-context reasoning, creating strong token connections that compose a superficial logical chain, rather than performing formal symbolic reasoning like humans.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs perform significantly better on reasoning tasks when semantics are consistent with commonsense compared to when semantics are decoupled (symbolic setting).
LLMs struggle to solve symbolic or counter-commonsense reasoning tasks by leveraging in-context new knowledge.
Semantic knowledge is easier for LLMs to memorize than symbolic knowledge, but updating semantic knowledge has a higher forgetting ratio due to stronger correlations.
LLMs' reasoning performance is inferior to logic-based symbolic methods across all tested reasoning tasks (deduction, induction, abduction).
