First, LLMs effectively encode the underlying relationships between analogous entities; both attributive and relational information propagate through mid-upper layers in correct cases, whereas reasoning failures reflect missing relational information within these layers. Second, unlike humans, LLMs often struggle not only when relational information is missing, but also when attempting to apply it to new entities. In such cases, strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer to a certain extent. Lastly, successful analogical reasoning in LLMs is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, whereas failures often reflect degraded or misplaced alignment. Overall, our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit emerging but limited capabilities in encoding and applying high-level relational concepts, highlighting both parallels and gaps with human cognition.

papers.title: Loop as a Bridge: Can Looped Transformers Truly Link Representation Space and Natural Language Outputs?
papers.research_question: Can Looped Transformers align linguistic verification output with representations? Can LTs enhance their introspective awareness on representations?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing loop iterations in Looped Transformers narrows the gap between self-verification and representation readout, but partly due to degradation of representation quality. Moreover, LTs only show introspective awareness in the final loop, not continuously across loops.
papers.conclusion: Current Looped Transformers do not yet achieve continuous introspection across loops, and the observed gap narrowing is partly driven by a degradation in representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
The accuracy of textual self-verification improves with more loop iterations.
The performance of representation-based linear probes declines with more loop iterations.
The gap between representation readout and self-verification narrows with more loops, but partly because of the decline in representation readout.
LTs are only aware of injected concepts when the injection occurs in the final loop, not in earlier loops.
papers.limitation: The experiments are a preliminary exploration conducted on a single specific implementation of LTs (Ouro), so the observed limitations should not be interpreted as intrinsic flaws of the general LTs paradigm.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit a gap between their internal knowledge and their explicit linguistic outputs. In this report, we empirically investigate whether Looped Transformers (LTs)--architectures that increase computational depth by iterating shared layers--can bridge this gap by utilizing their iterative nature as a form of introspection. Our experiments reveal that while increasing loop iterations narrows the gap, it is partly driven by a degradation of their internal knowledge carried by representations. Moreover, another empirical analysis suggests that current LTs' ability to perceive representations does not improve across loops; it is only present in the final loop. These results suggest that while LTs offer a promising direction for scaling computational depth, they have yet to achieve the introspection required to truly link representation space and natural language.

papers.title: From Emergence to Control: Probing and Modulating Self-Reflection in Language Models
papers.abstract: Self-reflection -- the ability of a large language model (LLM) to revisit, evaluate, and revise its own reasoning -- has recently emerged as a powerful behavior enabled by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). While self-reflection correlates with improved reasoning accuracy, its origin and underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, {\it we first show that self-reflection is not exclusive to RLVR fine-tuned models: it already emerges, albeit rarely, in pretrained models}. To probe this latent ability, we introduce Reflection-Inducing Probing, a method that injects reflection-triggering reasoning traces from fine-tuned models into pretrained models. This intervention raises self-reflection frequency of Qwen2.5 from 0.6\% to 18.6\%, revealing a hidden capacity for reflection. Moreover, our analysis of internal representations shows that both pretrained and fine-tuned models maintain hidden states that distinctly separate self-reflective from non-reflective contexts. Leveraging this observation, {\it we then construct a self-reflection vector, a direction in activation space associated with self-reflective reasoning}. By manipulating this vector, we enable bidirectional control over the self-reflective behavior for both pretrained and fine-tuned models. Experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks show that enhancing these vectors improves reasoning performance by up to 12\%, while suppressing them reduces computational cost, providing a flexible mechanism to navigate the trade-off between reasoning quality and efficiency without requiring additional training. Our findings further our understanding of self-reflection and support a growing body of work showing that understanding model internals can enable precise behavioral control.

papers.title: Does ChatGPT Have a Mind?
papers.research_question: This paper examines the question of whether Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT possess minds, focusing specifically on whether they have a genuine folk psychology encompassing beliefs, desires, and intentions.
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that LLMs have robust internal representations that satisfy various philosophical conditions, but the question of whether they have robust action dispositions for a full folk psychology remains open. It also contends that existing skeptical challenges to LLM representation do not survive philosophical scrutiny.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that there is strong evidence for LLM representation, but the question of whether they have full folk psychological states (beliefs and desires) remains open, particularly due to issues of action dispositions and stability.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs satisfy informational, causal, structural, and teleosemantic conditions on mental representation.
LLMs exhibit internal representations that carry information about the world and are causally effective in generating behavior.
LLMs show evidence of world models and structured representations, such as in color and direction concepts.
The behavior of LLMs in game environments suggests they may have action dispositions, but the evidence is not decisive.
Skeptical challenges (sensory grounding, stochastic parrots, memorization) do not undermine the case for LLM representation.
papers.limitation: LLM outputs are very sensitive to prompting, which makes it hard to see the LLM as taking a wide range of means to promote a unified goal.
future_direction: Exploring how stable LLM outputs are to a range of different prompting environments.
Investigating whether LLMs have anything analogous to enduring goals or values.
Further research on how LLM strategies in game environments change under different prompting conditions.
papers.abstract: This paper examines the question of whether Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT possess minds, focusing specifically on whether they have a genuine folk psychology encompassing beliefs, desires, and intentions. We approach this question by investigating two key aspects: internal representations and dispositions to act. First, we survey various philosophical theories of representation, including informational, causal, structural, and teleosemantic accounts, arguing that LLMs satisfy key conditions proposed by each. We draw on recent interpretability research in machine learning to support these claims. Second, we explore whether LLMs exhibit robust dispositions to perform actions, a necessary component of folk psychology. We consider two prominent philosophical traditions, interpretationism and representationalism, to assess LLM action dispositions. While we find evidence suggesting LLMs may satisfy some criteria for having a mind, particularly in game-theoretic environments, we conclude that the data remains inconclusive. Additionally, we reply to several skeptical challenges to LLM folk psychology, including issues of sensory grounding, the "stochastic parrots" argument, and concerns about memorization. Our paper has three main upshots. First, LLMs do have robust internal representations. Second, there is an open question to answer about whether LLMs have robust action dispositions. Third, existing skeptical challenges to LLM representation do not survive philosophical scrutiny.

papers.title: Understanding and Patching Compositional Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: What accounts for compositional reasoning failures in LLMs, and which parts of the LLMs are responsible for them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces CREME, a model-editing method that patches compositional reasoning errors by editing MHSA modules, based on the finding that implicit reasoning results are generated and leveraged in middle layers.
papers.conclusion: Successful compositional reasoning within LLMs hinges on its awareness of generating and leveraging implicit reasoning results, and MHSA modules in middle layers are responsible for this process. The proposed CREME method effectively patches such errors.
papers.key_findings:
Most compositional reasoning failures stem from improperly generated or leveraged implicit reasoning results.
Implicit reasoning results emerge in middle layers and causally affect explicit reasoning results.
MHSA modules in middle layers (e.g., 18/19-th layer) are responsible for generating and leveraging implicit reasoning results.
CREME effectively patches compositional reasoning errors and generalizes to paraphrased and related queries.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on Logit Lens, which is an approximate tool for interpreting hidden states.
Experiments are limited to 3B and 7B scale LLMs due to computational constraints.
Focus is on compositional reasoning of factual knowledge, not other task types.
future_direction: Validate conclusions on LLMs of larger scale.
Extend analysis to other types of compositional reasoning tasks, such as arithmetic reasoning.
papers.abstract: LLMs have marked a revolutonary shift, yet they falter when faced with compositional reasoning tasks. Our research embarks on a quest to uncover the root causes of compositional reasoning failures of LLMs, uncovering that most of them stem from the improperly generated or leveraged implicit reasoning results. Inspired by our empirical findings, we resort to Logit Lens and an intervention experiment to dissect the inner hidden states of LLMs. This deep dive reveals that implicit reasoning results indeed surface within middle layers and play a causative role in shaping the final explicit reasoning results. Our exploration further locates multi-head self-attention (MHSA) modules within these layers, which emerge as the linchpins in accurate generation and leveraing of implicit reasoning results. Grounded on the above findings, we develop CREME, a lightweight method to patch errors in compositional reasoning via editing the located MHSA modules. Our empirical evidence stands testament to CREME's effectiveness, paving the way for autonomously and continuously enhancing compositional reasoning capabilities in language models.

papers.title: Representation in large language models
papers.research_question: Is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, contrary to the look-up table view, and outlines how mechanistic interpretability methods can be used to study these representations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs do use representation-based information processing, and we can investigate these representations using mechanistic interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
The look-up table view of LLMs is inadequate because it cannot explain robust behavior.
Representations, as defined by four conditions (INFORMATION, EXPLOITABILITY, BEHAVIOR, ROLE), can explain robust behavior.
Mechanistic interpretability methods like probing and causal interventions can test for representations in LLMs.
papers.abstract: The extraordinary success of recent Large Language Models (LLMs) on a diverse array of tasks has led to an explosion of scientific and philosophical theorizing aimed at explaining how they do what they do. Unfortunately, disagreement over fundamental theoretical issues has led to stalemate, with entrenched camps of LLM optimists and pessimists often committed to very different views of how these systems work. Overcoming stalemate requires agreement on fundamental questions, and the goal of this paper is to address one such question, namely: is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up? This is a question about what kind of algorithm LLMs implement, and the answer carries serious implications for higher level questions about whether these systems have beliefs, intentions, concepts, knowledge, and understanding. I argue that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, and then I describe and defend a series of practical techniques for investigating these representations and developing explanations on their basis. The resulting account provides a groundwork for future theorizing about language models and their successors.

papers.title: Language Modeling with Learned Meta-Tokens
papers.research_question: How can language models be enhanced to capture long-range dependencies and improve length generalization using learned meta-tokens and a meta-attention mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces meta-tokens and a meta-attention mechanism for language model pre-training, which improves performance on recall-oriented tasks and enables length generalization by sharpening positional encoding and compressing context.
papers.conclusion: Pre-training LMs with meta-tokens offers a simple, data-efficient method to enhance long-context language modeling performance, while introducing new insights into the nature of their behavior towards length generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Meta-tokens improve performance on synthetic recall tasks compared to baselines.
Meta-tokens aid in length generalization up to 2x the pretraining context window.
Zeroing out positional encoding at meta-tokens can match or improve performance.
Meta-tokens sharpen positional encoding, reducing attention entropy.
Meta-tokens act as content-based landmarks, compressing preceding context.
papers.limitation: The study uses synthetic tasks and not real-world tasks; scaling to larger models and corpora is needed.
future_direction: Explore impact in pre-training larger models over longer context windows.
Study larger-scale corpora to see how rapidly models saturate on synthetic tasks.
Investigate hybrid attention methods like RNoPE for facilitating long-context modeling with meta-tokens.
papers.abstract: While modern Transformer-based language models (LMs) have achieved major success in multi-task generalization, they often struggle to capture long-range dependencies within their context window. This work introduces a novel approach using meta-tokens, special tokens injected during pre-training, along with a dedicated meta-attention mechanism to guide LMs to use these tokens. We pre-train a language model with a modified GPT-2 architecture equipped with meta-attention in addition to causal multi-head attention, and study the impact of these tokens on a suite of synthetic tasks. We find that data-efficient language model pre-training on fewer than 100B tokens utilizing meta-tokens and our meta-attention mechanism achieves strong performance on these tasks after fine-tuning. We suggest that these gains arise due to the meta-tokens sharpening the positional encoding. This enables them to operate as trainable, content-based landmarks, implicitly compressing preceding context and "caching" it in the meta-token. At inference-time, the meta-token points to relevant context, facilitating length generalization up to 2$\times$ its context window, even after extension with YaRN. We provide further evidence of these behaviors by visualizing model internals to study the residual stream, and assessing the compression quality by information-theoretic analysis on the rate-distortion tradeoff. Our findings suggest that pre-training LMs with meta-tokens offers a simple, data-efficient method to enhance long-context language modeling performance, while introducing new insights into the nature of their behavior towards length generalization.

papers.title: From Monolingual to Bilingual: Investigating Language Conditioning in Large Language Models for Psycholinguistic Tasks
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages, and how does language identity (monolingual vs bilingual prompting) affect their output behavior and internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that large language models condition their psycholinguistic behavior and internal representations on the language identity specified in the prompt, with differences between monolingual and bilingual prompting, offering insights into cross-linguistic cognition in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our results demonstrate that LLMs are not language-neutral. Instead, they respond to and encode language-specific cues in both their outputs and internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Both models adapt their outputs based on the linguistic identity embedded in the prompt.
Qwen shows greater sensitivity to prompt language and sharper behavioral distinctions between Dutch and Chinese than Llama.
Probing reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more linearly decodable in deeper layers.
Chinese prompts yield stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch prompts.
Bilingual prompting can introduce interference or noise, especially for low-resource languages like Dutch.
papers.limitation:
Focus on only three languages (English, Dutch, Chinese), limiting generalizability.
Only two LLMs are evaluated.
Tasks represent only a narrow slice of the psycholinguistic space.
future_direction: Expanding to include languages with different scripts, phonological systems, or morphological complexity (e.g., Arabic, Hindi, Finnish).
Incorporating a broader set of psycholinguistic phenomena, such as lexical decision making, semantic priming, syntactic ambiguity resolution, and metaphor comprehension.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong linguistic capabilities, but little is known about how they encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages. We investigate whether and how LLMs exhibit human-like psycholinguistic responses under different linguistic identities using two tasks: sound symbolism and word valence. We evaluate two models, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, under monolingual and bilingual prompting in English, Dutch, and Chinese. Behaviorally, both models adjust their outputs based on prompted language identity, with Qwen showing greater sensitivity and sharper distinctions between Dutch and Chinese. Probing analysis reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more decodable in deeper layers, with Chinese prompts yielding stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch. Our results demonstrate that language identity conditions both output behavior and internal representations in LLMs, providing new insights into their application as models of cross-linguistic cognition.

papers.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
papers.research_question: How can polysemantic interference structures in language models be exploited to manipulate model outputs, and do these interference patterns transfer across models of different scales and families?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that polysemantic interference structures in language models create a systematic vulnerability, and that interventions based on these structures, identified in small models, can transfer to larger instruction-tuned models for predictable behavioral control without requiring access to their internals.
papers.conclusion: Polysemantic interference reveals a systematic vulnerability in language models, and the generalization of these structures across scale and family challenges the view of polysemanticity as purely stochastic, offering new avenues for black-box control and theoretical insight into internal representation.
papers.key_findings:
Interventions leveraging polysemantic structures (feature-direction steering, token-gradient steering, prompt injection) can effectively manipulate model next-token predictions.
Polysemantic interference patterns are persistent across models: interventions distilled from small models (Pythia-70M, GPT-2-Small) transfer reliably to larger models (Llama-3.1, Gemma-2).
Many counterintuitive interference patterns are stable across models but remain largely opaque to human interpretation, suggesting models learn robust regularities not aligned with surface semantics.
Highly polysemantic neurons are more vulnerable to interventions; amplifying 'super-neurons' (activated by many features) strongly alters model behavior, while deactivating them has a reduced effect.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) whose outputs fluctuate with dimensionality and hyperparameters, yielding unstable features.
Interventions steer only one interference feature in one layer, while multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations could amplify and better obscure the effect.
Vulnerability is quantified solely via shifts in immediate next-token probabilities on two small base models, with only coarse transfer checks on larger instructed models.
future_direction: Establishing how these interventions alter non-trivial downstream tasks in bigger models.
Exploring multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations to amplify and better obscure intervention effects.
papers.abstract: Polysemanticity is pervasive in language models and remains a major challenge for interpretation and model behavioral control. Leveraging sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we map the polysemantic topology of two small models (Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small) to identify SAE feature pairs that are semantically unrelated yet exhibit interference within models. We intervene at four loci (prompt, token, feature, neuron) and measure induced shifts in the next-token prediction distribution, uncovering polysemantic structures that expose a systematic vulnerability in these models. Critically, interventions distilled from counterintuitive interference patterns shared by two small models transfer reliably to larger instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct), yielding predictable behavioral shifts without access to model internals. These findings challenge the view that polysemanticity is purely stochastic, demonstrating instead that interference structures generalize across scale and family. Such generalization suggests a convergent, higher-order organization of internal representations, which is only weakly aligned with intuition and structured by latent regularities, offering new possibilities for both black-box control and theoretical insight into human and artificial cognition.

papers.title: Self-correction is Not An Innate Capability in Language Models
papers.research_question: Is moral self-correction an innate capability of Large Language Models (LLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: Moral self-correction is not an inherent capability of LLMs, as they lack moral sensitivity and cannot effectively incorporate external feedback during the self-correction process.
papers.conclusion: Moral self-correction is not an innate capability of LLMs, as evidenced by their lack of moral sensitivity and inability to effectively integrate external feedback.
papers.key_findings:
Self-correction does not enhance LLMs' moral sensitivity in most evaluated scenarios.
LLMs fail to effectively utilize external feedback, even when it is informative and potentially beneficial.
External feedback exhibits non-positive effects on Chain-of-Thought (CoT), often reducing the activation of warrants within the CoT.
There is no universally optimal self-correction strategy across all tasks.
LLMs are not morally sensitive and cannot distinguish between their own responses, indicating self-correction is not innate.
papers.abstract: Although there has been growing interest in the self-correction capability of Large Language Models (LLMs), there are varying conclusions about its effectiveness. Prior research has largely concentrated on intrinsic self-correction, extrinsic self-correction, particularly the interplay between internal knowledge and external feedback, remains underexplored. In this paper, we aim to comprehensively investigate the underlying mechanism of moral self-correction by addressing a fundamental question: is moral self-correction an innate capability of LLMs? Specifically, we conduct: (1) a behavioral analysis of LLMs' moral sensitivity based on a self-distinguishing task; and (2) a mechanistic analysis of the hidden states to examine how key components of self-correction, such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and external feedback, interact to facilitate moral self-correction. Drawing on empirical evidence from both behavioral and mechanistic analyses, we demonstrate that moral self-correction is not an inherent capability of LLMs, as they are neither morally sensitive nor able to effectively incorporate external feedback during the self-correction process.

papers.title: Neural Meta-Symbolic Reasoning and Learning
papers.research_question: How can we build a neural meta-symbolic system that can reason and learn several tasks efficiently by using meta-level programming, enabling self-introspection and adaptation without modifying the internal reasoning system?
papers.core_contribution: We propose NEMESYS, the first neural meta-symbolic reasoning and learning system that performs differentiable forward reasoning using meta-level programs, enabling self-introspection and adaptation to multiple tasks without modifying the internal reasoning architecture.
papers.conclusion: NEMESYS represents a step towards more general and self-reflective AI systems by unifying differentiable reasoning and meta-level programming, opening avenues for differentiable meta-learning and program synthesis.
papers.key_findings:
NEMESYS achieves comparable or superior performance to object-level neuro-symbolic baselines on visual reasoning tasks like Kandinsky patterns and CLEVR-Hans.
NEMESYS can integrate additional functionalities like proof tree generation, relevance propagation, and infinite loop avoidance simply by changing meta-level programs.
NEMESYS can perform differentiable planning on visual scenes and causal reasoning with a differentiable do operator.
NEMESYS can learn meta-level program structures and parameters from examples using gradient descent, adapting to solve different tasks sequentially.
papers.limitation:
Scalability for large-scale meta programs is a limitation.
The system cannot handle real number calculations directly and uses weights associated with atoms as approximations.
For structure learning, candidates of meta-rules are provided, requiring prior knowledge.
future_direction: Integrate rule-learning techniques (e.g., mode declarations, meta-interpretive learning) to learn from less prior.
Explore providing properties about programs and injecting them into neural networks via algorithmic supervision.
Realize differentiable meta-learning, i.e., a reasoning system that learns how to perform reasoning better from experiences.
papers.abstract: Deep neural learning uses an increasing amount of computation and data to solve very specific problems. By stark contrast, human minds solve a wide range of problems using a fixed amount of computation and limited experience. One ability that seems crucial to this kind of general intelligence is meta-reasoning, i.e., our ability to reason about reasoning. To make deep learning do more from less, we propose the first neural meta-symbolic system (NEMESYS) for reasoning and learning: meta programming using differentiable forward-chaining reasoning in first-order logic. Differentiable meta programming naturally allows NEMESYS to reason and learn several tasks efficiently. This is different from performing object-level deep reasoning and learning, which refers in some way to entities external to the system. In contrast, NEMESYS enables self-introspection, lifting from object- to meta-level reasoning and vice versa. In our extensive experiments, we demonstrate that NEMESYS can solve different kinds of tasks by adapting the meta-level programs without modifying the internal reasoning system. Moreover, we show that NEMESYS can learn meta-level programs given examples. This is difficult, if not impossible, for standard differentiable logic programming

papers.title: Scaling Competence, Shrinking Reasoning: Cognitive Signatures in Language Model Learning
papers.research_question: How do reasoning tokens evolve during fine-tuning, and can they serve as indicators of learning stages?
papers.core_contribution: Reasoning tokens in language models expand, peak, and contract during fine-tuning, mirroring the Four Stages of Competence, and their dynamics can serve as metrics for diagnosing training stages and guiding early stopping.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning tokens serve as a dynamic scaffold during fine-tuning, providing insights into model learning dynamics and practical tools for diagnosing training progress and optimizing learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning token length increases with performance early in training, peaks at conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task.
Models retain task performance after training even when reasoning tokens are removed, indicating that reasoning scaffolds learning but becomes unnecessary once competence is acquired.
The progression of reasoning tokens aligns with the Four Stages of Competence framework from cognitive science.
Reasoning token dynamics can diagnose training stages, detect convergence, and inform early stopping criteria.
The pattern is consistent across multiple models and tasks including code generation, math problems, and logical question answering.
papers.limitation:
Reasoning token length and correctness are surface-level proxies for internal cognitive processes, and the use of competence stages is interpretive rather than diagnostic.
Experiments are limited to math, logic, and code generation tasks, and may not generalize to tasks with high ambiguity or contextual sensitivity.
The proposed metrics may be less stable in settings with noisy supervision, curriculum learning, or large-scale instruction tuning.
future_direction: Future work may formalize these analogies further or challenge them with deeper mechanistic analysis.
papers.abstract: We analyze reasoning in language models during task-specific fine-tuning and draws parallel between reasoning tokens--intermediate steps generated while solving problem and the human working memory. Drawing from cognitive science, we align training dynamics with the Four Stages of Competence: models initially produce incorrect outputs without reasoning, then begin reasoning (but still fail), eventually reason effectively, and finally solve tasks without explicit reasoning. We find that reasoning token length expands as performance improves, peaks at the stage of conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task. Notably, after training, models retain performance even when reasoning is removed--suggesting it scaffolded learning but is no longer needed. This progression offers actionable insights: reasoning token dynamics can serve as a signal for diagnosing training stage, identifying convergence, and guiding early stopping. We propose metrics to track this trajectory and argue that reasoning behavior is valuable for understanding and optimizing reasoning model training.

papers.title: Beyond Induction Heads: In-Context Meta Learning Induces Multi-Phase Circuit Emergence
papers.research_question: How is meta-learning ability in in-context learning acquired during training, specifically through the dynamics of the model's internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: Meta-learning ability in in-context learning is acquired through multiple phases, each with a distinct circuit emerging, contrasting with the single-phase change observed in induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Multi-phase circuit emergence underlies the acquisition of meta-learning capabilities in in-context learning, and these findings help bridge the gap between controlled mechanistic interpretability experiments and practical large language model behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The model undergoes three learning phases (Non-Context, Semi-Context, Full-Context) with distinct circuits emerging in each phase.
Sudden jumps in accuracy align with the abrupt emergence of these circuits.
The Semi-Context Circuit explains the random-label robustness phenomenon observed in large language models.
In multi-head settings, circuits emerge in parallel, leading to smoother accuracy improvements while hidden circuit changes still occur.
Similar circuit patterns (chunk example in early layers, label attention in later layers) are observed in pretrained models like GPT2-XL on real-world tasks.
papers.limitation: The work uses a simplified transformer model and synthetic data, which may not fully capture the complexity of real large language model behaviors.
future_direction: Connecting controlled experiments in mechanistic interpretability to realistic use-cases of large language models.
Bridging geometric perspectives (like Local Learning Coefficient) with mechanistic circuit analyses to enrich interpretability methodologies.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models exhibit In-Context Learning (ICL), where predictions are made adaptively based on context. While prior work links induction heads to ICL through a sudden jump in accuracy, this can only account for ICL when the answer is included within the context. However, an important property of practical ICL in large language models is the ability to meta-learn how to solve tasks from context, rather than just copying answers from context; how such an ability is obtained during training is largely unexplored. In this paper, we experimentally clarify how such meta-learning ability is acquired by analyzing the dynamics of the model's circuit during training. Specifically, we extend the copy task from previous research into an In-Context Meta Learning setting, where models must infer a task from examples to answer queries. Interestingly, in this setting, we find that there are multiple phases in the process of acquiring such abilities, and that a unique circuit emerges in each phase, contrasting with the single-phases change in induction heads. The emergence of such circuits can be related to several phenomena known in large language models, and our analysis lead to a deeper understanding of the source of the transformer's ICL ability.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Enable Scalable and Reliable Circuit Identification in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and robustly discover interpretable circuits in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method for circuit identification using discrete sparse autoencoders trained on attention head outputs, which is more efficient and robust than existing techniques.
papers.conclusion: Discrete sparse autoencoders offer a scalable, efficient, and robust approach for circuit identification in large language models, providing a promising direction for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The method outperforms or matches state-of-the-art circuit identification techniques (ACDC, HISP, SP) in precision and recall on three tasks (IOI, Greater-than, Docstring).
The method is robust to hyperparameter choices and requires only 5-10 text examples per task to learn robust representations.
The identified circuits can match or even outperform the full model's performance on the specific tasks with fewer components.
The method can identify negative components in circuits (e.g., negative name-mover heads in IOI) that other algorithms struggle to find.
The process is significantly faster, reducing runtime from hours to seconds compared to existing methods.
papers.limitation: The method currently only analyzes attention heads and not other components like MLP layers, which may be important for some circuits (e.g., Greater-than).
future_direction: Extending the method to analyze MLP layers and other model components.
Applying the method to larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the use of vector-quantized variational autoencoders (VQ-VAEs) as an alternative to sparse autoencoders.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces an efficient and robust method for discovering interpretable circuits in large language models using discrete sparse autoencoders. Our approach addresses key limitations of existing techniques, namely computational complexity and sensitivity to hyperparameters. We propose training sparse autoencoders on carefully designed positive and negative examples, where the model can only correctly predict the next token for the positive examples. We hypothesise that learned representations of attention head outputs will signal when a head is engaged in specific computations. By discretising the learned representations into integer codes and measuring the overlap between codes unique to positive examples for each head, we enable direct identification of attention heads involved in circuits without the need for expensive ablations or architectural modifications. On three well-studied tasks - indirect object identification, greater-than comparisons, and docstring completion - the proposed method achieves higher precision and recall in recovering ground-truth circuits compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while reducing runtime from hours to seconds. Notably, we require only 5-10 text examples for each task to learn robust representations. Our findings highlight the promise of discrete sparse autoencoders for scalable and efficient mechanistic interpretability, offering a new direction for analysing the inner workings of large language models.

papers.title: Can Language Model Understand Word Semantics as A Chatbot? An Empirical Study of Language Model Internal External Mismatch
papers.research_question: How does the understanding of word semantics differ between internal representations and external outputs in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds a discrepancy between internal and external representations in language models for word semantics understanding, with internal probes consistently outperforming external queries, indicating that model knowledge is not fully propagated to outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study highlights a mismatch between internal and external representations in language models, suggesting that improving truthfulness could enhance their reliability in applications.
papers.key_findings:
Probe accuracy is consistently higher than query accuracy across all models and benchmarks.
In the WiC benchmark, query accuracy is near random (49-53%), while probe accuracy is significantly higher (up to 65%).
For NER, encoder-based models like BERT achieve high probe F1 scores (96%), but query performance is very low.
Finetuning (e.g., Flan-T5) improves query accuracy but still does not match probe accuracy.
Probes are better calibrated than queries, with models like BERT and T5 showing better calibration.
papers.limitation:
Due to limitations in hardware resources and budget constraints, the number of models included is relatively limited, which might affect the generalizability of the findings.
Unable to explore more complex model architectures due to restricted computational capacity.
future_direction: Expand the scope of model selection and explore more diverse and intricate models with additional resources.
papers.abstract: Current common interactions with language models is through full inference. This approach may not necessarily align with the model's internal knowledge. Studies show discrepancies between prompts and internal representations. Most focus on sentence understanding. We study the discrepancy of word semantics understanding in internal and external mismatch across Encoder-only, Decoder-only, and Encoder-Decoder pre-trained language models.

papers.title: Superscopes: Amplifying Internal Feature Representations for Language Model Interpretation
papers.research_question: How can we interpret internal representations (like MLP outputs and hidden states) in language models that are not interpretable with existing self-interpretation methods, by amplifying weak features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Superscopes, a method that amplifies weak features in internal representations (MLP outputs and hidden states) to enable their interpretation via self-interpretation methods like Patchscopes, without requiring additional training.
papers.conclusion: Superscopes extends Patchscopes by amplifying internal representations, enabling interpretation of previously uninterpretable MLP outputs and hidden states, and draws a parallel to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models.
papers.key_findings:
Amplifying MLP outputs reveals meaningful interpretations that are not accessible with standard Patchscopes.
Amplifying hidden states can reveal interpretations in layers before contextualization occurs.
The amplification technique is analogous to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models, as both amplify directional shifts.
The Superscopes framework can automatically identify optimal amplification factors for interpretation.
The method demonstrates that weak features in internal representations can be amplified to reveal semantic content.
papers.limitation:
The method does not currently handle attention outputs, which may have a denser superposition of features.
The method for selecting the optimal amplifier may not be fully effective and could be improved.
future_direction: Extracting meaning from attention outputs.
Developing more effective approaches for selecting the optimal amplifier.
Exploring alternative ways to amplify meaning within Superscopes, such as using a different base vector for patching.
papers.abstract: Understanding and interpreting the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains an open challenge. Patchscopes introduced a method for probing internal activations by patching them into new prompts, prompting models to self-explain their hidden representations. We introduce Superscopes, a technique that systematically amplifies superposed features in MLP outputs (multilayer perceptron) and hidden states before patching them into new contexts. Inspired by the "features as directions" perspective and the Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) approach from diffusion models, Superscopes amplifies weak but meaningful features, enabling the interpretation of internal representations that previous methods failed to explain-all without requiring additional training. This approach provides new insights into how LLMs build context and represent complex concepts, further advancing mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: When Thinking Backfires: Mechanistic Insights Into Reasoning-Induced Misalignment
papers.abstract: With the growing accessibility and wide adoption of large language models, concerns about their safety and alignment with human values have become paramount. In this paper, we identify a concerning phenomenon: Reasoning-Induced Misalignment (RIM), in which misalignment emerges when reasoning capabilities strengthened-particularly when specific types of reasoning patterns are introduced during inference or training. Beyond reporting this vulnerability, we provide the first mechanistic account of its origins. Through representation analysis, we discover that specific attention heads facilitate refusal by reducing their attention to CoT tokens, a mechanism that modulates the model's rationalization process during inference. During training, we find significantly higher activation entanglement between reasoning and safety in safety-critical neurons than in control neurons, particularly after fine-tuning with those identified reasoning patterns. This entanglement strongly correlates with catastrophic forgetting, providing a neuron-level explanation for RIM.

papers.title: On Representational Dissociation of Language and Arithmetic in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What about the language-thought dissociation in large language models? Specifically, are language and arithmetic inputs encoded in separate regions in LLMs' internal representation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that language and arithmetic inputs are encoded in completely separated regions in LLMs' internal representation space, and that math word problems form a separate cluster, suggesting fine-grained modularity beyond a coarse language-arithmetic dissociation.
papers.conclusion: This study explores the representational dissociation between language and arithmetic stimuli in LLMs, setting a direction to bridge neuroscientific perspectives with LLM internal analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Language and arithmetic equations are encoded in completely separated regions across all layers of LLMs.
The separation is not due to token differences, as spelled-out equations are also separated from language inputs.
Math word problems (GSM8K) form a separate cluster from both language and arithmetic regions.
The arithmetic region activated with primitive stimuli is not used in more complex arithmetic-involved tasks.
There are numerous arithmetic regions for different task formats, indicating fine-grained modularity.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to geometrical properties of the representation space; causal analysis is needed to align with actual abilities.
The generality of findings could be enhanced with other methodologies, such as gradient descent, magnitude of neuron activations, or activation probability.
The topic should be addressed through different experimental designs, e.g., ablating language learning scenarios.
future_direction: Incorporate alternative approaches to identify language and arithmetic regions, such as gradient descent, magnitude of neuron activations, or activation probability.
Conduct causal analysis to test whether the observed geometrical dissociation aligns with actual abilities.
Contextualize the results with existing LM-brain alignment studies.
Address the learnability of specific abilities through different experimental designs, e.g., ablating language learning scenarios.
papers.abstract: The association between language and (non-linguistic) thinking ability in humans has long been debated, and recently, neuroscientific evidence of brain activity patterns has been considered. Such a scientific context naturally raises an interdisciplinary question -- what about such a language-thought dissociation in large language models (LLMs)? In this paper, as an initial foray, we explore this question by focusing on simple arithmetic skills (e.g., $1+2=$ ?) as a thinking ability and analyzing the geometry of their encoding in LLMs' representation space. Our experiments with linear classifiers and cluster separability tests demonstrate that simple arithmetic equations and general language input are encoded in completely separated regions in LLMs' internal representation space across all the layers, which is also supported with more controlled stimuli (e.g., spelled-out equations). These tentatively suggest that arithmetic reasoning is mapped into a distinct region from general language input, which is in line with the neuroscientific observations of human brain activations, while we also point out their somewhat cognitively implausible geometric properties.

papers.title: A Self-Organizing Computational Neural Network Architecture with Applications to Sensorimotor Grounded Linguistic Grammar Acquisition
papers.research_question: How can a self-organizing neural network architecture acquire linguistic grammar and demonstrate systematicity, particularly in sensorimotor grounded language acquisition?
papers.core_contribution: This paper develops a novel unsupervised neural network architecture called Chimaera that can acquire separate representations for conceptual and grammatical information, enabling systematic language acquisition and semantic bootstrapping with sensorimotor grounded input.
papers.conclusion: The Chimaera network is capable of acquiring linguistic grammar and demonstrating systematicity, supporting the semantic bootstrapping hypothesis of language acquisition.
papers.key_findings:
The Chimaera network can simultaneously store explicit representations of conceptual and grammatical information through a hybrid of self-organizing maps and Hebbian associative networks.
With recurrent processing, the Chimaera network can handle ambiguous grammars and deep n-back transitions efficiently.
Using a co-occurrence-based activation function with sensorimotor grounded input, the network performs semantic bootstrapping to acquire part-of-speech categories.
The network demonstrates systematic behavior on a benchmark grammar test and extends knowledge to novel sensorimotor-grounded words.
It outperforms previous supervised and unsupervised models like Frank (2006) and Farkas & Crocker (2008) in acquiring systematicity.
papers.limitation:
Representing data vectors can be challenging for the network, affecting input representation.
Topography can affect activation and learning dynamics in the self-organizing map.
In feed-forward mode, the network requires many layers to resolve deeply ambiguous grammars, which is computationally inefficient.
future_direction: Extending the network to operate at the lexical level rather than only grammatical category level.
Applying the architecture to other models and domains beyond language acquisition.
Investigating the plausibility of the semantic co-occurrence metric in biological systems.
papers.abstract: Connectionist models of language acquisition typically have difficulty with systematicity, or the ability for the network to generalize its limited experience with language to novel utterances. In this way, connectionist systems learning grammar from a set of example sentences tend to store a set of specific instances, rather than a generalized abstract knowledge of the process of grammatical combination. Further, recent models that do show limited systematicity do so at the expense of simultaneously storing explicit lexical knowledge, and also make use of both developmentally-implausible training data and biologically-implausible learning rules. Consequently, this research program develops a novel unsupervised neural network architecture, and applies this architecture to the problem of systematicity in language models. In the first of several studies, a connectionist architecture capable of simultaneously storing explicit and separate representations of both conceptual and grammatical information is developed, where this architecture is a hybrid of both a self-organizing map and an intra-layer Hebbian associative network. Over the course of several studies, this architecture's capacity to acquire linguistic grammar is evaluated, where the architecture is progressively refined until it is capable of acquiring a benchmark grammar consisting of several difficult clausal sentence structures - though it must acquire this grammar at the level of grammatical category, rather than the lexical level. The final study bridges the gap between the lexical and grammatical category levels, and develops an activation function based on a semantic feature co-occurrence metric. In concert with developmentally-plausible sensorimotor grounded conceptual representations, it is shown that a network using this metric is able to undertake a process of semantic bootstrapping, and successfully acquire separate explicit representations at the level of the concept, part-of-speech category, and grammatical sequence. This network demonstrates broadly systematic behaviour on a difficult test of systematicity, and extends its knowledge of grammar to novel sensorimotor-grounded words.

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.

papers.title: Auxiliary Metrics Help Decoding Skill Neurons in the Wild
papers.research_question: Can auxiliary metrics help identify skill-related neurons in large language models for tasks involving multiple skills, fine-grained linguistic heuristics, and without explicit meta-labels?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to identify skill neurons in LLMs by correlating neuron activations on trained soft prompts with auxiliary metrics, enabling analysis in multi-skill tasks and discovery of unknown shortcuts without manual token aggregation.
papers.conclusion: The method consistently identifies sparse neurons corresponding to fine-grained linguistic skills and previously unknown heuristics, aiding in understanding skill specialization within LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
The method can detect skill-related neurons in open-ended generation tasks when provided with explicit meta labels.
It can disen tangle and isolate neurons specialized for fine-grained linguistic heuristics within a uniform task setting like natural language inference.
It can identify skill neurons without explicit meta-labels, revealing previously unknown shortcuts such as last-digit patterns in arithmetic reasoning.
Neurons with high correlation to auxiliary metrics are sparse, with only a small subset showing substantial correlation.
Activation distributions of selected neurons differ clearly between skills or heuristics, providing interpretable evidence.
papers.limitation:
Depends on the quality of prompt tuning and the availability of clear auxiliary metrics.
Designed to discover correlational signatures, not causal influences on model behaviors.
future_direction: Exploring the causal influence of identified neurons on model behaviors.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities across a wide range of tasks, yet their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque. In this paper, we introduce a simple, lightweight, and broadly applicable method with a focus on isolating neurons that encode specific skills. Building upon prior work that identified "skill neurons" via soft prompt training on classification tasks, our approach extends the analysis to complex scenarios involving multiple skills. We correlate neuron activations with auxiliary metrics -- such as external labels and the model's own confidence score -- thereby uncovering interpretable and task-specific behaviors without the need for manual token aggregation. We empirically validate our method on tasks spanning open-ended text generation and natural language inference, demonstrating its ability to detect neurons that not only drive known skills but also reveal previously unidentified shortcuts in arithmetic reasoning on BigBench.

papers.title: Interpreting Language Models Through Concept Descriptions: A Survey
papers.research_question: The paper surveys the field of concept descriptions for model components, aiming to answer questions about common methods and data sources, best practices for evaluation, observed trends, and key gaps and future directions.
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first survey of the emerging field of concept descriptions for model components and abstractions, charting methods, evaluation techniques, and datasets, and identifies a growing demand for rigorous causal evaluation and provides a roadmap for future research.
papers.conclusion: The use of LLMs to generate concept descriptions is a notable step towards demystifying LLMs, with a trajectory from labeling neurons to abstractions and maturing evaluation methods, but the path to verifiable causal mechanisms is not yet fully paved and costs and faithfulness concerns remain.
papers.key_findings:
Recognition of neuron polysemanticity has driven adoption of model abstractions like Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and frameworks for multiple concepts per feature.
Evaluation of concept descriptions is maturing, with multi-faceted metrics assessing predictive power, input accuracy, and causal faithfulness.
The field is moving from labeling individual neurons to higher-level abstractions like SAEs and circuits.
There is a need for more rigorous causal evaluation and standardized benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
Focus limited to natural language concept descriptions for internal model components and abstractions, excluding other interpretability work.
Substantial computational and financial costs associated with the methods surveyed.
Focus on English-language models and text corpora, with generalization to other languages being an open question.
future_direction: Scaling automated description methods to circuits.
Applying concept description methods to new data domains and modalities.
Analyzing the interpreters (LLMs) themselves to understand biases and limitations in generated descriptions.
papers.abstract: Understanding the decision-making processes of neural networks is a central goal of mechanistic interpretability. In the context of Large Language Models (LLMs), this involves uncovering the underlying mechanisms and identifying the roles of individual model components such as neurons and attention heads, as well as model abstractions such as the learned sparse features extracted by Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). A rapidly growing line of work tackles this challenge by using powerful generator models to produce open-vocabulary, natural language concept descriptions for these components. In this paper, we provide the first survey of the emerging field of concept descriptions for model components and abstractions. We chart the key methods for generating these descriptions, the evolving landscape of automated and human metrics for evaluating them, and the datasets that underpin this research. Our synthesis reveals a growing demand for more rigorous, causal evaluation. By outlining the state of the art and identifying key challenges, this survey provides a roadmap for future research toward making models more transparent.

papers.title: Linguistic generalization and compositionality in modern artificial neural networks
papers.research_question: How do modern deep artificial neural networks achieve linguistic generalization and productivity, and do they rely on systematic compositional rules?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reviews evidence that modern deep neural networks can achieve sophisticated linguistic generalization without relying on systematic compositional rules, and argues this behavior offers a new perspective on computational strategies for linguistic productivity relevant to cognitive science.
papers.conclusion: Modern deep neural networks are proficient at language processing and exhibit subtle grammatical generalization, yet they do not rely on systematic compositional rules, offering a comparative perspective for studying linguistic productivity and non-systematic generalization patterns in human language.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks can capture abstract, structure-dependent grammatical generalizations (e.g., long-distance number agreement) even in nonsensical sentences.
These networks fail at systematic compositional generalization in controlled tasks like the SCAN benchmark (e.g., jump and around-right splits).
Some architectures (e.g., convolutional seq2seq) show partial success on compositional splits but without systematicity, making errors uniformly across composition frames.
In communication games, neural networks can develop productive but non-compositional codes that generalize as well as compositional ones.
Analysis of a network's internal circuitry (e.g., ablation studies) suggests it develops genuine grammatical processing mechanisms rather than relying on surface heuristics.
papers.limitation: Our current understanding of the strategies learned by these networks is very limited, and better analytical tools are needed to uncover the mechanisms behind the dissociation of productive grammatical competence and systematic compositionality.
future_direction: Develop better analytical tools to uncover the mechanisms that lead to the detected dissociation of productive grammatical competence and systematic compositionality.

Investigate whether making neural networks more compositional, for example by means of more structured modular architectures, will make them more adaptive and faster at learning without sacrificing generality.

Use progress in understanding the linguistic capabilities of neural networks to make precise predictions about the origin, scope, and mechanics of non-systematic productive phenomena in human language.
papers.abstract: In the last decade, deep artificial neural networks have achieved astounding performance in many natural language-processing tasks. Given the high productivity of language, these models must possess effective generalization abilities. It is widely assumed that humans handle linguistic productivity by means of algebraic compositional rules: are deep networks similarly compositional? After reviewing the main innovations characterizing current deep language-processing networks, I discuss a set of studies suggesting that deep networks are capable of subtle grammar-dependent generalizations, but also that they do not rely on systematic compositional rules. I argue that the intriguing behaviour of these devices (still awaiting a full understanding) should be of interest to linguists and cognitive scientists, as it offers a new perspective on possible computational strategies to deal with linguistic productivity beyond rule-based compositionality, and it might lead to new insights into the less systematic generalization patterns that also appear in natural language. This article is part of the theme issue 'Towards mechanistic models of meaning composition'.

papers.title: Intra-neuronal attention within language models Relationships between activation and semantics
papers.research_question: To what extent do neurons in language models exhibit intra-neuronal attention, i.e., a homomorphic relationship between activation segments and categorical segments of tokens?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds a weak but consistent relationship between activation segments and categorical segments in neurons, particularly for tokens with very high activation levels, suggesting a form of intra-neuronal attention.
papers.conclusion: Intra-neuronal attention exists in language model neurons, albeit weakly, and contributes to the progressive formation of high-level categorical abstractions through restructuring in later layers.
papers.key_findings:
Overall categorical homogeneity within activation clusters is low.
Categorical homogeneity increases with activation level: tokens with higher activation tend to be more semantically similar.
The relationship between activation and categorical segments is tenuous and only strong for the highest activation tokens.
Intra-neuronal attention enables categorical restructuring processes in subsequent layers, contributing to higher-level abstractions.
papers.limitation: The use of GPT-2XL embeddings is a specific operational choice that does not represent an absolute semantic ontology, so interpretations are contingent on this particular semantic space.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the ability of perceptron-type neurons in language models to perform intra-neuronal attention; that is, to identify different homogeneous categorical segments within the synthetic thought category they encode, based on a segmentation of specific activation zones for the tokens to which they are particularly responsive. The objective of this work is therefore to determine to what extent formal neurons can establish a homomorphic relationship between activation-based and categorical segmentations. The results suggest the existence of such a relationship, albeit tenuous, only at the level of tokens with very high activation levels. This intra-neuronal attention subsequently enables categorical restructuring processes at the level of neurons in the following layer, thereby contributing to the progressive formation of high-level categorical abstractions.

papers.title: Towards Uncovering How Large Language Model Works: An Explainability Perspective
papers.research_question: How can explainability techniques uncover the internal mechanisms of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: This survey paper provides a systematic overview of existing explainability techniques, including mechanistic interpretability and representation engineering, to uncover the inner workings of large language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that explainability techniques like mechanistic interpretability and representation engineering are crucial for understanding LLMs, but there are still challenges such as scalability and evaluation of explanations.
papers.limitation: The survey does not explore the complete landscape of relevant XAI methods for understanding LLMs, due to space constraints.
future_direction: Developing scalable techniques to analyze and interpret the intricate knowledge structures embedded within LLMs.
Revealing the intricate mechanisms that give rise to advanced reasoning capabilities in LLMs.
Fully leveraging insights from explainability to develop techniques that can substantially improve LLM performance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have led to breakthroughs in language tasks, yet the internal mechanisms that enable their remarkable generalization and reasoning abilities remain opaque. This lack of transparency presents challenges such as hallucinations, toxicity, and misalignment with human values, hindering the safe and beneficial deployment of LLMs. This paper aims to uncover the mechanisms underlying LLM functionality through the lens of explainability. First, we review how knowledge is architecturally composed within LLMs and encoded in their internal parameters via mechanistic interpretability techniques. Then, we summarize how knowledge is embedded in LLM representations by leveraging probing techniques and representation engineering. Additionally, we investigate the training dynamics through a mechanistic perspective to explain phenomena such as grokking and memorization. Lastly, we explore how the insights gained from these explanations can enhance LLM performance through model editing, improve efficiency through pruning, and better align with human values.

papers.title: Discovering Salient Neurons in Deep NLP Models
papers.research_question: Can we identify subsets of neurons that learn specific linguistic properties, and how is linguistic knowledge localized, distributed, and affected by fine-tuning in NLP models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Linguistic Correlation Analysis (LCA) for extracting salient neurons in NLP models, revealing that linguistic knowledge is localized in lower layers for basic properties and distributed in higher layers for complex concepts, with variations across models and during fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The LCA method provides insights into how linguistic knowledge is encoded in neurons, showing localization patterns and redistribution during fine-tuning, with implications for model understanding and transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
Small subsets of neurons can predict different linguistic tasks.
Neurons for basic lexical information are localized in lower layers, while those for complex concepts are in higher layers.
Linguistic information is redundantly preserved across neurons.
During transfer learning, salient linguistic neurons relocate to lower layers in some models like RoBERTa and XLNet.
Multilingual models exhibit similar neuron distribution for concepts across different languages.
future_direction: Pinpointing specific concepts regressed to lower layers versus those retained in higher layers during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: While a lot of work has been done in understanding representations learned within deep NLP models and what knowledge they capture, little attention has been paid towards individual neurons. We present a technique called as Linguistic Correlation Analysis to extract salient neurons in the model, with respect to any extrinsic property - with the goal of understanding how such a knowledge is preserved within neurons. We carry out a fine-grained analysis to answer the following questions: (i) can we identify subsets of neurons in the network that capture specific linguistic properties? (ii) how localized or distributed neurons are across the network? iii) how redundantly is the information preserved? iv) how fine-tuning pre-trained models towards downstream NLP tasks, impacts the learned linguistic knowledge? iv) how do architectures vary in learning different linguistic properties? Our data-driven, quantitative analysis illuminates interesting findings: (i) we found small subsets of neurons that can predict different linguistic tasks, ii) with neurons capturing basic lexical information (such as suffixation) localized in lower most layers, iii) while those learning complex concepts (such as syntactic role) predominantly in middle and higher layers, iii) that salient linguistic neurons are relocated from higher to lower layers during transfer learning, as the network preserve the higher layers for task specific information, iv) we found interesting differences across pre-trained models, with respect to how linguistic information is preserved within, and v) we found that concept exhibit similar neuron distribution across different languages in the multilingual transformer models. Our code is publicly available as part of the NeuroX toolkit.

papers.title: Can Edge Probing Tasks Reveal Linguistic Knowledge in QA Models?
papers.research_question: Does fine-tuning for QA tasks change the encoding of linguistic knowledge in encoders as measured by edge probing tests, and why might EP tests fail to reflect such changes?
papers.core_contribution: Edge probing test results do not significantly change after fine-tuning QA models, but this is due to dataset biases in EP tests; when biases are corrected, improvements in linguistic knowledge encoding are observed.
papers.conclusion: EP tests may not accurately capture changes in linguistic knowledge due to dataset biases, and fine-tuned models do improve when these biases are addressed, suggesting that models acquire linguistic skills as expected.
papers.key_findings:
EP test results remain stable after fine-tuning on QA tasks, even when models are expected to learn linguistic skills.
Fine-tuned encoders show no significant difference in EP tests compared to base encoders, even on skill-specific datasets like Quoref.
EP tests are susceptible to dataset biases, such as memorization heuristics, which can be exploited without using good representations.
When EP test datasets are corrected for biases, fine-tuned encoders demonstrate improved performance over base encoders.
The consistency of EP test results in prior work is explained by dataset biases rather than a lack of change in linguistic knowledge.
papers.limitation: EP tests have dataset biases that may prevent them from accurately reflecting changes in linguistic knowledge
future_direction: Identify exact reasoning steps in QA models through post-hoc explainability methods to study alignment with human reasoning.
papers.abstract: There have been many efforts to try to understand what grammatical knowledge (e.g., ability to understand the part of speech of a token) is encoded in large pre-trained language models (LM). This is done through `Edge Probing' (EP) tests: supervised classification tasks to predict the grammatical properties of a span (whether it has a particular part of speech) using only the token representations coming from the LM encoder. However, most NLP applications fine-tune these LM encoders for specific tasks. Here, we ask: if an LM is fine-tuned, does the encoding of linguistic information in it change, as measured by EP tests? Specifically, we focus on the task of Question Answering (QA) and conduct experiments on multiple datasets. We find that EP test results do not change significantly when the fine-tuned model performs well or in adversarial situations where the model is forced to learn wrong correlations. From a similar finding, some recent papers conclude that fine-tuning does not change linguistic knowledge in encoders but they do not provide an explanation. We find that EP models themselves are susceptible to exploiting spurious correlations in the EP datasets. When this dataset bias is corrected, we do see an improvement in the EP test results as expected.

papers.title: Differentiation and Specialization of Attention Heads via the Refined Local Learning Coefficient
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in a transformer language model differentiate and specialize during training, as revealed by refined local learning coefficients?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces refined local learning coefficients (rLLCs) as a principled, quantitative toolkit for developmental interpretability, revealing how attention heads differentiate and specialize during training and enabling the discovery of a novel multigram circuit.
papers.conclusion: Refined local learning coefficients provide a powerful toolkit for developmental interpretability, revealing the interplay between data distributional structure, loss landscape geometry, learning dynamics, and the resulting computational structure in neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Weight-refined LLCs (wrLLCs) reveal how attention heads differentiate into distinct functional types (e.g., induction heads, multigram heads) over the course of training.
Data-refined LLCs (drLLCs) show how heads specialize to different data distributions, such as one induction head specializing more to code.
The combination of refined LLCs leads to the identification of a novel multigram circuit involving coordination between layer 0 and layer 1 multigram heads.
The developmental perspective (evolution over time) is crucial for understanding the emergence of internal structure; point estimates at the end of training are insufficient.
Refined LLCs provide a quantitative link between data distributional structure, geometric properties of the loss landscape, learning dynamics, and emergent computational structures.
papers.limitation:
The justification of the LLC estimator presumes that w* is a local minima of the population loss, but there is no clear way to ascertain this in practice, and estimates are often performed during training where this is unlikely.
The ground truth LLC is unknown, so the accuracy of estimated LLC values cannot be guaranteed, though there is reason to believe the ordinality is correct.
future_direction: Establishing the correspondence between data distributional structure, geometric properties of the loss landscape, learning dynamics, and emergent computational structures in neural networks.
papers.abstract: We introduce refined variants of the Local Learning Coefficient (LLC), a measure of model complexity grounded in singular learning theory, to study the development of internal structure in transformer language models during training. By applying these \textit{refined LLCs} (rLLCs) to individual components of a two-layer attention-only transformer, we gain novel insights into the progressive differentiation and specialization of attention heads. Our methodology reveals how attention heads differentiate into distinct functional roles over the course of training, analyzes the types of data these heads specialize to process, and discovers a previously unidentified multigram circuit. These findings demonstrate that rLLCs provide a principled, quantitative toolkit for \textit{developmental interpretability}, which aims to understand models through their evolution across the learning process.
